claims.text: The starting alloy is equiatomic Mo–Fe–Cr–Co–Ni.
Arc melting and homogenization produce the starting alloy as a single-phase solid solution.
Partial substitution of Fe or Co by Mn changes the alloy's effective electron count.
The change in effective electron count alters the density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level modulate electron–phonon coupling.
Modification of electron–phonon coupling changes the superconducting pairing interaction and shifts Tc.
Fe or Co will be replaced by 10–30 at.% Mn while every constituent remains above 5 at.%.
Using identical arc-melting, homogenization, and annealing conditions will ensure comparable phase purity and microstructure.
Mn-substituted alloys will exhibit a systematic and reproducible Tc shift relative to the equiatomic baseline.
Tunneling spectroscopy will show changes in the density of states near the Fermi energy corresponding to the Tc shifts.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the substituted material remains a single-phase solid solution with every element above 5 at.%.
The proposed mechanism assumes that the alloys remain in the conventional BCS regime.
The proposed mechanism assumes that phase stability is maintained during Mn substitution.
The magnitude and sign of the predicted Tc shift are unknown.
Tc will be measured independently by electrical resistivity and magnetic susceptibility.
X-ray diffraction and atom-probe tomography will be used to assess phase purity and compositional homogeneity.
A lack of systematic variation in both Tc and the near-Fermi-level density of states across the substitution series would falsify the hypothesis.
Tc shifts attributable to phase separation or compositional inhomogeneity rather than controlled electron-count changes would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The baseline contains only 20 at.% Fe and 20 at.% Co. If 10–30 at.% means absolute alloy concentration, replacing 30 at.% of either donor is impossible, and retaining the donor above 5 at.% permits less than 15 at.% absolute replacement.

If 10–30 at.% means 10–30% of the donor element rather than absolute alloy concentration, Mn would be only 2–6 at.%; most of that range violates the requirement that every element remain above 5 at.%.

Partial Mn-for-Fe or Mn-for-Co substitution adds Mn while retaining the original five elements, producing a six-element alloy, whereas the boundary describes a five-element solid solution. This is inconsistent unless 'five-element' was intended to mean 'at least five elements.'
